Lucas Lindeboom
loo'kəs lin'də-bōm
n. (Lucas Lindeboom, 1845–1933, professor at Kampen, critic of Kuyper, and founder of Christian care for the mentally ill in the Netherlands)
Latin Lucas, from Greek Loukas, of Lucania; Dutch lindeboom, linden tree.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lucas Lindeboom was a minister of the Seceder churches who became a professor at the Theological School at Kampen in 1883 and taught there for decades. He is remembered in two connections. In theology, he was the most persistent critic within the Reformed churches of Abraham Kuyper's system: he resisted the doctrine of presumptive regeneration, by which the children of the covenant were to be regarded as regenerate until they showed otherwise; he opposed Kuyper's teaching of justification from eternity; and after the union of 1892 he fought to keep Kampen as the churches' own school rather than see theological training absorbed into Kuyper's Free University. In mercy, he was the moving spirit behind the association founded in 1884 for the Christian care of the insane, which opened the first Reformed psychiatric institutions in the Netherlands at a time when the mentally ill were commonly confined in prisons and poorhouses. He believed that the church which confesses the doctrines of grace must show their fruit to the weakest: “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me” (Mat 25:40).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an asylum as a place of refuge, and insanity as derangement of the intellect.

expand to see more

ASY'LUM, n. A place of retreat and security; a refuge; an institution for the protection or relief of the unfortunate.

INSAN'ITY, n. The state of being unsound in mind; derangement of intellect; madness.

REGENERA'TION, n. In theology, new birth by the grace of God; that change by which the will and natural enmity of man to God are subdued.

Key Scripture

Mat 25:40 — "And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."

Jam 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

1Th 5:21 — "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good."

Mal 2:7 — "For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts."

Modern Corruption

A Kampen professor who checked Kuyper's speculations and opened asylums for the insane.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error Lindeboom resisted was speculative: a theology that reasons from God's decree to conclusions Scripture does not draw, so that infants are presumed regenerate and the elect justified before they believe. His rule was the apostle's, “Prove all things” (1Th 5:21), and the Reformed churches eventually adopted the guarded Conclusions of Utrecht in 1905, which restrained the speculations he had opposed.

The second lesson is that orthodoxy and mercy are not alternatives. The man who would not yield an inch on justification spent decades building homes for the mentally ill, because “Pure religion and undefiled before God” (Jam 1:27) visits the afflicted. The modern habit of setting doctrinal precision against compassion has no purchase on his life.

Usage

"“one of the least of these my brethren” (Mat 25:40) — the asylums of 1884."

"“Pure religion and undefiled” (Jam 1:27) — mercy joined to doctrine."

"“Prove all things” (1Th 5:21) — his answer to Kuyper's speculations."
